title: Incremental XML Stream Framing Over Fragmented TCP Sockets
solutionExplanation:
The framer handles arbitrary byte fragmentation:
1. extract_loop trims leading whitespace using ASCII byte comparisons (32, 13, 10, 9) and repeatedly calls try_extract_frame until no more complete XML elements can be formed.
2. If the buffer begins with <stream:stream, it extracts the opening tag up to >.
3. For child tags, it parses the TagName, checks if the tag is self-closing (<tag ... />), and if not, searches for the matching closing tag </tag>.
4. If a tag is incomplete, it returns need_more and copies the remaining slice using binary:copy/1 to prevent sub-binary leaks.

otpDocCards.description: Extracts a slice from Subject as a sub-binary.
Forces clean allocation of remaining unparsed buffer bytes.
otpDocCards.complexityNote: Prevents long-lived connection processes from retaining socket buffers.

mentalModelCheck.question: Why MUST an incremental XML stream framer call binary:copy/1 when extracting attribute values or stanza bodies from a TCP buffer?

options.label: To prevent sub-binary retention leaks where a tiny extracted slice pins a large 64 KB refc binary in process heap memory.
options.explanation: Sub-binaries retain reference counters to their parent binary. binary:copy/1 copies the small slice and releases the refc binary.

options.label: Because Erlang binaries are immutable and cannot be read without copying.
options.explanation: Binaries are read directly via pattern matching; binary:copy/1 is used specifically for memory unpinning.

options.label: Because gen_statem will reject uncopied binaries with a badmatch error.
options.explanation: gen_statem accepts any term; memory management is an engineering optimization.

options.label: To convert the binary to a null-terminated C string.
options.explanation: Erlang binaries are length-prefixed, not null-terminated.
